correctness.rationale: In coordinates M={y=0}, P=[0:1:0], a conic has binary restriction proportional to L_(i−1)L_i since its two distinct contacts already exhaust the intersection with M. Its y-linear coefficient vanishes identically since both tangent lines contain P. Smoothness forces the y² and product coefficients nonzero; the normalized y²+c_iL_(i−1)L_i is smooth even in characteristic two (the only possible common zero of the two independent partials in x,z would be P, which is off the conic). The consecutive difference is L_i times a binary linear form; the tangent factor has order two and the other has order two exactly when it is proportional to L_i, otherwise it is a unit at p_i. This gives a nonzero recurrence; the product of consecutive determinant ratios is (−1)^n. Its consistency is sufficient, because the unordered point pairs on M distinguish the smooth conics, and Bézout counts the full intersection. Multiplying the coefficients by a common nonzero scalar is absorbed by y-scaling over the algebraic closure, and every projectivity of M lifts preserving P. The claimed quotient is thus exactly the stated set of marked classes M_{0,n}(k). In characteristic two any telescoped difference is a nonzero square of a binary linear form; on its line through P either conic restricts to y²+d s², a nonzero square. The conic-line intersection is a unique double point, so the squared difference forces fourfold contact, whether or not that point is on M.
residual_risks: The assertion concerns projective classes over algebraically closed fields, not rational descent or an identification of moduli stacks or stabilizer group schemes.

originality.rationale: A known complex four-cycle overlaps a fixed-length example, but that and the comparison papers do not establish the characteristic-dependent all-length classification or realization and uniqueness for arbitrary marked configurations. The distinct contribution credited is the simultaneous parity and marked orbit theorem in arbitrary characteristic. The common-nucleus square-difference mechanism in characteristic two is elementary once the incidence is understood and does not by itself carry this verdict.

value.rationale: A natural geometric incidence problem has a complete realization criterion and a marked orbit classification, not merely examples or a numerical bound. The criterion changes in characteristic two, where nonadjacent pairs additionally acquire maximal contact. This gives usable control of the incidence geometry while isolating precisely which conditions are needed.
residual_risks: No classification of singularity schemes or freeness of the full arrangement follows.
